questions.stem: The state of matter that takes the volume of the whole container is
explanation_steps: Solids keep their own shape and volume; liquids keep their volume but take the shape of the container.
Gas particles move freely through the entire space of the container, so a gas takes both the shape and the volume of the container. Answer: D.
tips: 'Fills the whole container' = gas. 'Takes the shape but not the volume' = liquid.

similar_questions.stem: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
explanation_steps: A liquid keeps its volume but flows to take the shape of its container. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Silver has 47 protons and a mass number of 108. The number of neutrons are
explanation_steps: Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number (number of protons).
tips: Mass number counts protons + neutrons; the electrons are not counted.

similar_questions.stem: An atom of zinc has 30 protons and a mass number of 65. How many neutrons does it have?
explanation_steps: Neutrons = 65 − 30 = 35. Answer: B.

questions.stem: How many atoms are present in the chemical formula of ammonium dichromate, (NH₄)₂Cr₂O₇?
explanation_steps: The bracket (NH₄) is multiplied by 2: 2 N + 8 H = 10 atoms.
Cr₂O₇: 2 Cr + 7 O = 9 atoms.
Total = 10 + 9 = 19 atoms. Answer: D.
tips: A subscript outside a bracket multiplies every atom inside the bracket.

similar_questions.stem: How many atoms are in one formula unit of Ca₃(PO₄)₂?
explanation_steps: 3 Ca + 2 × (1 P + 4 O) = 3 + 2 + 8 = 13 atoms. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about Mendeleev's periodic table?

options.A: Properties of elements are the periodic function of their mass number.
options.B: Elements were classified into groups and periods.
options.C: The position of hydrogen was not clearly indicated.
options.E: There was disorder in atomic mass for some pair of elements.

explanation_steps: Mendeleev arranged the elements in groups (columns) and periods (rows) – B is true.
The textbook lists the defects of his table: the position of hydrogen, isotopes and a disorder in atomic mass for certain pairs of elements – so C and E are true statements about the table.
Because isotopes have different masses but identical properties, Mendeleev's table had no proper place for them. 'Isotopes were placed properly' is therefore false. Answer: D.
Note: the textbook states Mendeleev's law as 'properties are a periodic function of their atomic MASS'; option A says 'mass number', which is loosely worded but is clearly meant as the atomic mass.
tips: Mendeleev's three defects: hydrogen, isotopes, disorder in atomic mass (e.g. Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I).
Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of ATOMIC NUMBER.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following was a defect of Mendeleev's periodic table?

options.B: He left gaps for undiscovered elements
options.C: Isotopes of an element had no proper position
options.D: He predicted the properties of gallium

explanation_steps: Gaps and predictions were strengths of the table; groups and periods are its structure.
Isotopes (different masses, same properties) could not be placed properly – a defect. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two options are strictly untrue: D (isotopes had no proper place – the textbook defect) and A, which says 'mass number' where Mendeleev's law (textbook p.7) uses 'atomic mass'. D is keyed; A is also accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: The type of covalent bond formed by sharing four electrons is
explanation_steps: Each shared electron pair (2 electrons) is one covalent bond.
Four shared electrons = two shared pairs = a double bond (e.g. O=O, C=C). Answer: B.
tips: Electrons shared: 2 → single, 4 → double, 6 → triple.

similar_questions.stem: How many electrons are shared in the triple bond of N≡N?
explanation_steps: A triple bond = 3 shared pairs = 6 electrons. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Acetic acid, CH₃COOH, the acid used to prepare vinegar, is
explanation_steps: Only the hydrogen of the –COOH group ionises: CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻.
The three H atoms of the CH₃ group are bonded to carbon and are not acidic.
One ionisable H per molecule = monoprotic. Answer: D.
tips: Count only the ionisable (acidic) hydrogens, not all hydrogens in the formula.

similar_questions.stem: Sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, is classified as
explanation_steps: H₂SO₄ can release two H⁺ ions per molecule. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The following statements describe liquid solutions, except

options.A: they have variable compositions of solute and solvent.
options.B: their physical properties are the same with those of their pure solvents.
options.D: filtration cannot be used to separate the substances that make up the solutions.

explanation_steps: A solution is a homogeneous mixture: its composition can vary (A true), it is clear (C true) and the solute passes through filter paper (D true).
Dissolving a solute changes the properties of the solvent – boiling point is raised, freezing point and vapour pressure lowered – so B is false. Answer: B.
tips: Colligative properties are the proof that a solution's properties differ from the pure solvent's.

similar_questions.stem: Which property of a sugar solution is different from that of pure water?
explanation_steps: Dissolved sugar raises the boiling point (boiling-point elevation). Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following is not true about energy.

options.A: Kinetic energy is due to the motion of particles of a substance.
options.B: Potential energy is due to the position of particles contained in a substance.
options.C: Chemical energy is a form of potential energy.
options.D: Thermal energy is a form of kinetic energy.
options.E: Electrical energy is a form of potential energy.

explanation_steps: The textbook: kinetic energy is due to motion; its forms include thermal energy and electrical energy.
Potential energy is due to position; its forms include chemical and gravitational energy.
So electrical energy is kinetic, not potential – E is not true. Answer: E.
tips: Electrical energy = moving electrons → kinetic.

similar_questions.stem: According to the Grade 10 textbook, which is a form of potential energy?
explanation_steps: Chemical energy is stored in the positions of particles (bonds) – potential energy. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 5.1 Energy transformation – kinetic and potential energy

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not correct about a rate of a reaction?

options.A: It refers to the speed of a chemical reaction.
options.B: It can be measured by change in temperature.
options.C: It depends on the concentration of reactants.

explanation_steps: Rate of reaction = speed of the reaction, measured as change in concentration (or another measurable property) per unit time (A true).
It depends on concentration, temperature, surface area and catalysts (C true), and it decreases as reactants are used up.
So a rate is never 'always the same' – D is incorrect. Answer: D.
(B is unusual wording; heat change can be followed for some reactions, but D is the clearly false statement.)
tips: A reaction is fastest at the start, when reactant concentrations are highest.

similar_questions.stem: Which factor does NOT change the rate of the reaction of zinc granules with dilute HCl?
explanation_steps: Temperature, concentration, surface area and catalysts all affect rate; the colour of the flask does not. Answer: E.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it

questions.stem: Electrolysis is useful for
explanation_steps: Impure copper is refined by electrolysis with an impure copper anode and pure copper cathode.
Very reactive metals (K, Na) are extracted by electrolysis of their molten compounds.
Chlorine is prepared by electrolysis of brine; electroplating (e.g. zinc/chromium/tin coatings) protects iron from rusting.
All four are applications. Answer: E.
tips: Electrolysis applications: refining, extraction of reactive metals, chlor-alkali, electroplating.

similar_questions.stem: Which process does NOT use electrolysis?

options.D: Extracting iron in a blast furnace

explanation_steps: Iron is extracted by reduction with carbon (coke) in a blast furnace, not by electrolysis. Answer: D.

questions.stem: According to Charles's Law, as the volume of a gas increases, the
explanation_steps: Charles's law: at constant pressure (and amount), V ∝ T (Kelvin).
So a larger volume corresponds to a higher absolute temperature. Answer: E.
Option C states the condition of the law (constant pressure), not the relationship; E is the best answer, but C is not a false statement.
tips: Boyle: P–V at constant T. Charles: V–T at constant P. Gay-Lussac: P–T at constant V.

similar_questions.stem: At constant pressure, a gas occupies 2.0 L at 300 K. What is its volume at 450 K?
explanation_steps: V₂ = V₁T₂/T₁ = 2.0 × 450/300 = 3.0 L. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: C ('pressure remains the same') is the condition under which Charles's law holds, so it is also a true statement. E (the V–T relationship) is keyed; C is also accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following molecules has different geometry?
explanation_steps: CO₂, BeH₂ and C₂H₂ have two electron domains around each central atom and no lone pairs → linear (180°).
H₂O has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs on O → bent/angular (104.5°). Answer: C.
tips: Lone pairs on the central atom bend the molecule.

similar_questions.stem: Which molecule is bent?
explanation_steps: SO₂ has a lone pair on S, so it is bent; the others are linear. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The manufacturing of sulphuric acid involves

options.C: diluting fuming sulphuric acid with water.
options.D: bubbling sulphur trioxide through concentrated sulphuric acid.

explanation_steps: Contact process stages (textbook): 1) S + O₂ → SO₂ (burning sulphur in air);
2) 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅;
3) SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ → oleum H₂S₂O₇ (fuming sulphuric acid);
4) oleum is diluted with water → H₂SO₄. All four steps are listed. Answer: E.
tips: SO₃ is not dissolved directly in water – it forms a corrosive acid mist.

similar_questions.stem: In the contact process, the catalyst used to convert SO₂ to SO₃ is
explanation_steps: Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, catalyses 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about copper?

options.A: It is a very reactive metal.
options.B: There is a large deposit of copper in Eritrea.
options.C: It is useful for conducting electricity.
options.D: Brass and bronze are alloys of copper.
options.E: It is used in making coins.

explanation_steps: Copper is below hydrogen in the activity series – it does not displace H₂ from dilute acids and reacts only slowly with oxygen. It is not very reactive.
Eritrea has large copper deposits (e.g. Bisha, Debarwa); copper is an excellent electrical conductor; brass (Cu–Zn) and bronze (Cu–Sn) are copper alloys; it is used for coins.
Answer: A.
tips: Low reactivity is exactly why copper is used for water pipes, coins and wires.

similar_questions.stem: Which metal does NOT react with dilute hydrochloric acid?
explanation_steps: Copper lies below hydrogen in the activity series. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following organic compounds is unsaturated hydrocarbon?
explanation_steps: Alkanes, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, are saturated: C₄H₁₀ (n=4), C₂H₆ (n=2), C₁₂H₂₆ (n=12) all fit.
C₂H₂ fits CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ – ethyne (acetylene) with a C≡C triple bond → unsaturated. Answer: C.
tips: Test with the formula: H = 2n+2 → saturated alkane; fewer H → unsaturated.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
explanation_steps: C₃H₆ = CₙH₂ₙ (propene, C=C). The others are alkanes. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about nuclear fission?

options.A: It involves the splitting of small atoms into two or more smaller ones.
options.C: A small energy is released during fission.

explanation_steps: Fission is the splitting of a HEAVY nucleus (e.g. U-235) into smaller parts, releasing a LARGE amount of energy – A and C are false.
The fission fragments (e.g. Kr, Ba, Sr, Xe isotopes) and neutrons are highly radioactive – B is true.
Stars are powered by fusion, and fission is normally induced in reactors (neutron bombardment) – D and E are not the intended properties. Answer: B.
tips: Fission = heavy splits; fusion = light joins (stars).

similar_questions.stem: The energy of the Sun comes from
explanation_steps: Stars fuse light nuclei (hydrogen → helium). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not matter?
explanation_steps: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
Carbon dioxide, eggs and even an electron (it has mass, 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg) are matter.
Light is a form of energy (electromagnetic waves) and has no rest mass – not matter. Answer: D.
tips: Energy forms (light, heat, sound) are not matter.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an example of matter?
explanation_steps: Heat is energy, not matter. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The electron configuration of ⁴⁵₂₁X is
explanation_steps: Atomic number 21 → 21 electrons (element scandium, the first transition element).
After 2, 8, 8 (argon) the 4s orbital fills first (2 electrons: K, Ca); the 21st electron goes into the 3d subshell, i.e. the third shell.
Sc: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹4s² → shells 2, 8, 9, 2. Answer: B.
tips: 2, 8, 8, 3 is a common trap – from Sc onward the third shell expands up to 18.

similar_questions.stem: What is the shell configuration of titanium (Z = 22)?
explanation_steps: Ti: [Ar]3d²4s² → 2, 8, 10, 2. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Modern periodic table – electron configuration and transition elements

questions.stem: When oxygen reacts with a hydrocarbon to form water and carbon dioxide, the reaction is called a
explanation_steps: Burning a substance in oxygen with release of heat and light is combustion; complete combustion of a hydrocarbon gives CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Answer: D.
tips: Hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O is the signature of combustion.

similar_questions.stem: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O is an example of
explanation_steps: Propane burns in oxygen to CO₂ and water – combustion. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a transition element?
explanation_steps: Transition (d-block) elements of period 4 run from Z = 21 to Z = 30.
Ca and K are s-block, Al and Ar p-block; scandium (Z = 21) is the first transition element. Answer: B.
tips: First transition series: Sc (21) … Zn (30).

similar_questions.stem: Which atomic number belongs to a transition element?
explanation_steps: Z = 26 is iron, in the d-block (21–30). Answer: C.

questions.stem: The forces of attraction do all of the following, except they

options.D: strengthen chemical bonds in a compound.

explanation_steps: Textbook: intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) hold atoms together within a molecule (A); intermolecular forces keep molecules together (B); an ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between positive and negative ions (C).
The forces of attraction ARE the chemical bonds; the textbook does not describe them as something that 'strengthens' bonds, so D is the statement that does not fit. Answer: D (keyed).
Confidence is low: a teacher may argue that stronger attraction means stronger bonds, making E ('None of the above') the intended answer.
tips: Intra- = within a molecule (bonds); inter- = between molecules.

similar_questions.stem: The forces that hold water molecules to each other in liquid water are
explanation_steps: Forces between separate molecules are intermolecular (here hydrogen bonds). Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

questions.review_flag: Ambiguous item: A–C are clearly done by forces of attraction; D ('strengthen chemical bonds') is vague and E ('None of the above') is also defensible. D keyed, E accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: A solution with relatively small amount of solute compared to the amount of solvent is
explanation_steps: Dilute and concentrated describe the relative amount of solute: little solute in much solvent = dilute. Answer: B.
Saturated/unsaturated compare the dissolved amount with the maximum that can dissolve (solubility), which the stem does not mention.
tips: Dilute/concentrated ≠ unsaturated/saturated: a saturated solution of a slightly soluble salt can still be dilute.

similar_questions.stem: A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature is
explanation_steps: Maximum dissolved amount at that temperature = saturated. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.2 Types of solutions – dilute and concentrated

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a reversible reaction?

options.A: Equilibrium mixture of reactants and products.
options.B: No visible change in the concentration of the reactants and products.
options.C: The rates of forward and backward reactions are equal.
options.D: There is constant concentrations of the reactants and products.

explanation_steps: A reversible reaction in a closed system reaches dynamic equilibrium: both reactants and products are present (A),
the forward and backward rates are equal (C), so the concentrations stay constant (D) and no visible change occurs (B).
All options describe the equilibrium state of a reversible reaction. Answer: E.
tips: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at equal rates.

similar_questions.stem: At chemical equilibrium,

options.B: the concentrations of reactants and products are always equal
options.C: the forward and reverse rates are equal

explanation_steps: Equilibrium: rates equal, concentrations constant (not necessarily equal). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest pH?
explanation_steps: Vinegar (acetic acid), lemon juice, citric acid and orange juice are acidic (pH < 7).
Milk of magnesia is a suspension of Mg(OH)₂, a base (pH ≈ 10). Highest pH. Answer: C.
tips: Highest pH = most basic.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance has the lowest pH?
explanation_steps: Lemon juice is acidic (pH ≈ 2); the others are neutral or basic. Answer: D.

questions.stem: During exothermic reaction,

options.C: heat of the products is greater than that of the reactants.
options.D: heat of the reactants is greater than that of the products.

explanation_steps: In an exothermic reaction heat is released to the surroundings, so the vessel gets warmer (A, B false).
The released heat is the difference H(reactants) − H(products); therefore the reactants have more heat content than the products (ΔH < 0). Answer: D.
tips: Exothermic: ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) < 0.

similar_questions.stem: For an endothermic reaction,

options.C: the products have more heat content than the reactants

explanation_steps: Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH > 0, H(products) > H(reactants). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about oxidation?

options.A: It is removal of oxygen from a substance.
options.B: It is the addition of hydrogen to a substance.
options.C: It is the gaining of electrons from a substance.
options.D: It results in the increase of oxidation number.

explanation_steps: Oxidation = addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number.
A, B and C describe reduction. Answer: D.
tips: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

similar_questions.stem: In which change is the first species reduced?
explanation_steps: Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons; its oxidation number falls from +2 to 0 → reduction. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Monoclinic sulphur is soluble in
explanation_steps: Both crystalline allotropes of sulphur (rhombic and monoclinic) are insoluble in water but dissolve in carbon disulphide, CS₂. Answer: B.
tips: Sulphur allotropes crystallise from CS₂ solution – remember 'sulphur loves carbon disulphide'.

similar_questions.stem: Rhombic sulphur changes into monoclinic sulphur at about
explanation_steps: The transition temperature given in the textbook is 96 °C. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
textbook_ref.note: The textbook's own review question (p.114) asks in what rhombic sulphur is soluble, with carbon disulphide as the answer option.

questions.stem: Which of the following pair of metals reacts so vigorously with oxygen?
explanation_steps: Na and K are at the top of the activity series; they tarnish instantly in air and burn vigorously, so they are stored under oil.
Zn/Fe react slowly; Pb, Hg, Ag, Au are unreactive. Answer: B.
tips: Top of the activity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

similar_questions.stem: Which metal is stored under paraffin oil because it reacts rapidly with air and water?
explanation_steps: Sodium is highly reactive (top of the activity series). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not true about ideal gases?

options.A: The force of attraction among the molecules is negligible.
options.B: The volume occupied by the molecules is negligible.
options.C: They obey all gas laws only at high temperature and at a low pressure.
options.D: They obey the ideal gas equation.

explanation_steps: An ideal gas is defined by negligible molecular volume and negligible attraction (A, B true) and obeys PV = nRT (D true) under ALL conditions.
It is REAL gases that behave ideally only at high temperature and low pressure. So C is not true of ideal gases. Answer: C.
tips: Trap: 'high T and low P' describes when real gases approximate ideal behaviour.

similar_questions.stem: Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at
explanation_steps: At low T and high P molecules are close together, so their volume and attractions matter. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following represent the shape of a unit cell, except
explanation_steps: Fig. 1.9 of the Grade 12 textbook shows the seven unit-cell shapes: simple cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral, monoclinic, triclinic and hexagonal.
'Trigonal' is not among the textbook's names. Answer: D.
Note: in crystallography 'trigonal' is another name for the rhombohedral system; the item follows the textbook's list.
tips: Learn the textbook's seven: cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral, monoclinic, triclinic, hexagonal.

similar_questions.stem: Which unit cell has a = b = c and α = β = γ = 90°?
explanation_steps: All edges equal and all angles 90° → cubic. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
textbook_ref.note: The seven shapes are named in Fig. 1.9 (an image, checked on the rendered page).

questions.review_flag: 'Trigonal' and 'rhombohedral' denote the same crystal system in crystallography; D is keyed only because the textbook (Fig. 1.9) names the shape 'rhombohedral' and never 'trigonal'.

questions.stem: 3-Pentanone is a five carbon atom with functional group of
explanation_steps: The ending '-one' denotes a ketone (C=O bonded to two carbons). 3-Pentanone is CH₃CH₂–CO–CH₂CH₃ (diethyl ketone). Answer: D.
tips: Suffixes: -ol alcohol, -al aldehyde, -one ketone, -oic acid, -oate ester.

similar_questions.stem: The compound CH₃CH₂CHO is
explanation_steps: –CHO at the end of the chain = aldehyde → propanal. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The application of nuclear chemistry is to

options.A: spot broken bones and dental problems.
options.B: destroy bacteria, insects and fungi in food.

explanation_steps: Radiation and radioisotopes are used in medicine (X-ray/radio-imaging of bones and teeth), in food irradiation (killing bacteria, insects, fungi), in forensic analysis and in sterilising/disinfecting water.
All are applications. Answer: E.
tips: When every option is a genuine use, choose 'All of the above'.

similar_questions.stem: Cobalt-60 is used in hospitals mainly to
explanation_steps: γ-rays from Co-60 destroy cancer cells (radiotherapy). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.6 Commercial and medicinal uses of radioactivity

questions.stem: In Eritrea, table salt is produced by
explanation_steps: Sea water is let into shallow salt pans along the Red Sea coast (Massawa, Assab); the sun evaporates the water and salt crystals are left. Answer: C.
tips: Evaporation recovers a dissolved solid; distillation recovers the liquid.

similar_questions.stem: Which method separates dissolved copper(II) sulphate from its aqueous solution to obtain the solid?
explanation_steps: Evaporating the water leaves the dissolved solid. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
textbook_ref.note: Evaporation as a separation method is in the text; the Eritrean salt pans are general knowledge.

questions.stem: The mass number and atomic number of an atom X are 31 and 15, respectively. The ion of atom X is
explanation_steps: Z = 15 → electron arrangement 2, 8, 5 (phosphorus), 5 valence electrons.
A nonmetal gains 3 electrons to reach the argon configuration 2, 8, 8 → X³⁻ (phosphide ion). Answer: C.
tips: Group 15 nonmetals form 3− ions; the mass number is not needed.

similar_questions.stem: An element Y has atomic number 16. Its common ion is
explanation_steps: 2, 8, 6 → gains 2 electrons → Y²⁻. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 2 – Atomic Structure and Chemical Bonding
textbook_ref.note: Ion formation by gaining/losing electrons to reach an octet (Grade 9 Unit 2); page approximate.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the highest molecular mass? [At. Mass: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16]
explanation_steps: Highest: C₄H₁₀ (58). Answer: E.
tips: Write each sum quickly; do not assume the formula with oxygen is heaviest.

similar_questions.stem: Which has the lowest molecular mass? [H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16]
explanation_steps: NH₃ 17, H₂O 18, CH₄ 16, N₂ 28, CO 28. Lowest CH₄. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following statements is true about the classification of elements in the periodic table. [At. number: Li = 3, C = 6, N = 7, O = 8, F = 9, Na = 11, Mg = 12, Cl = 17, K = 19]

options.A: Na and Mg belong to the same group.
options.B: O and N fall in the same period.
options.C: Li and C belong to the same group.
options.D: F and Cl are in the same period.
options.E: Na and K are in the same period.

explanation_steps: Electron arrangements: Li 2,1; C 2,4; N 2,5; O 2,6; F 2,7; Na 2,8,1; Mg 2,8,2; Cl 2,8,7; K 2,8,8,1.
Same number of shells = same period; same number of valence electrons = same group.

questions.stem: Write 6.1 one similarity and 6.2 two differences between graphite and diamond. (3 points)
questions.answer:
6.1 Similarity: both are crystalline allotropes of pure carbon (both burn in oxygen to give only CO₂; both have covalently bonded carbon atoms and high melting points).
6.2 Differences: (i) diamond is the hardest substance known, graphite is soft and greasy; (ii) diamond is a poor conductor of electricity, graphite is a good conductor; also: diamond is colourless and transparent, graphite greyish-black and opaque; density 3.5 vs 2.3 g/cm³; in diamond each C is bonded to four others in a 3-D tetrahedral network, in graphite each C is bonded to three others in flat layers held by weak forces.

Differences come from the arrangement of atoms (textbook Table 3.1): hardness, conductivity, appearance, density, structure.
marking_points: Similarity: allotropes of carbon / same element / both give CO₂ on burning (1)
tips: Link each property to structure: free (delocalised) electrons in graphite layers → conduction; strong 3-D network in diamond → hardness.

similar_questions.stem: Explain why graphite is used as a lubricant and as electrodes, whereas diamond is used in cutting tools.

questions.stem: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous when inhaled? (2 points)
questions.answer: Carbon monoxide combines with the haemoglobin of the blood much more readily (about 200–300 times more strongly) than oxygen, forming stable carboxyhaemoglobin. The blood can then no longer carry oxygen to the body cells, so the cells are starved of oxygen, leading to headache, unconsciousness and death. It is especially dangerous because it is colourless and odourless and cannot be detected; about 0.5 % in air is lethal.
explanation_steps: Normally haemoglobin + O₂ → oxyhaemoglobin, which delivers oxygen to the cells.
CO is similar in size to O₂ and binds to haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, blocking oxygen transport (textbook G11 p.77).
CO cannot be seen or smelt, so victims are unaware of the danger.
marking_points: CO combines with haemoglobin (forms carboxyhaemoglobin) more strongly than O₂ (1)
So blood cannot transport oxygen to the cells → suffocation/death (1)
(Colourless and odourless – cannot be detected: supporting point)
tips: Never run charcoal stoves (mogogo/fornello) or engines in closed rooms.

similar_questions.stem: Why should a charcoal stove never be used for heating in a closed room?
similar_questions.answer: Charcoal burns incompletely in limited oxygen, producing carbon monoxide; this colourless, odourless gas combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin and prevents oxygen transport, which can kill the people in the room.
explanation_steps: Limited air → incomplete combustion 2C + O₂ → 2CO.
CO blocks haemoglobin.

questions.stem:
8.1 What is metallurgy? (1 point)
8.2 Differentiate between roasting and calcination process. (3 points)
questions.answer:
8.1 Metallurgy is the science and technology of extracting metals from their ores and refining (purifying) them for use.
8.2 Roasting: a sulphide ore is heated strongly in excess air, converting it to the metal oxide and releasing SO₂, e.g. 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Calcination: a carbonate (or hydrated) ore is heated strongly in a limited supply of air (or its absence), decomposing it to the metal oxide and releasing CO₂ (or water), e.g. ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.

subparts.question: What is metallurgy?
subparts.answer: The science and technology of extracting metals from their ores and purifying them.

subparts.question: Differentiate between roasting and calcination.
subparts.answer: Roasting: sulphide ore heated in excess air → oxide + SO₂. Calcination: carbonate ore heated in limited air → oxide + CO₂.
steps: Compare ore type, air supply and product gas; an example equation for each.

explanation_steps: Textbook G11 p.124: 'Metallurgy is the science and technology of separating metals from their ores…'.

Textbook G11 p.127: sulphide ores are converted into oxides by strong heating in excess air (roasting); carbonate ores are changed into oxides by strong heating in limited air (calcining or calcination).
Differences: type of ore (sulphide vs carbonate), air supply (excess vs limited), gas released (SO₂ vs CO₂).
marking_points: 8.2 roasting: sulphide ore heated in excess air → oxide (1)
8.2 calcination: carbonate ore heated in limited/no air → oxide + CO₂ (1)
8.2 correct example/equation or gas released for either (1)
tips: Roasting – sulphide – excess air – SO₂. Calcination – carbonate – limited air – CO₂.

Complete the following reactions: (5 points)
9.1 CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ + HBr → ______
9.2 ______ --(H₂SO₄)-→ CH₃CH₂CH=CH₂ + H₂O
9.3 CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + ______ → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOCH₃ + H₂O
9.4 ______ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O
9.5 The reaction in 9.4 is called ______ reaction.
questions.answer:
9.1 CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ (2-bromobutane)
9.2 CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (butan-1-ol)
9.3 CH₃OH (methanol)
9.4 CH₃COOH (ethanoic/acetic acid)
9.5 neutralization (acid–base) reaction

subparts.question: The reaction in 9.4 is called ___ reaction.

explanation_steps: 9.1 HBr adds across the C=C (hydrohalogenation). By Markovnikov's rule the H goes to the terminal CH₂ (the carbon that already has more H) and Br to C-2 → 2-bromobutane.
9.2 Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water (dehydration) from an alcohol to form an alkene; the alcohol with the OH on C-1 gives but-1-ene cleanly → butan-1-ol.
9.3 The product is methyl butanoate, an ester: acid + alcohol → ester + water, so the missing reactant is methanol, CH₃OH.
9.4 CH₃COONa is sodium ethanoate; acid + base → salt + water, so the acid is CH₃COOH.
9.5 An acid reacting with a base to give a salt and water is a neutralization reaction.
marking_points: 9.2: accept butan-2-ol with ½ (gives mainly but-2-ene)
tips: Esters: the alcohol part is named first (methyl), the acid part second (butanoate).
The Grade 12 textbook only shows HBr + ethene; Markovnikov's rule (H to the carbon with more H) decides the product for unsymmetrical alkenes.

explanation_steps: (a) Markovnikov addition puts Cl on the middle carbon.
(b) Esterification: acid + alcohol → ester + water.
